newsitem.title: USA: Refiling of Foster Wheeler lawsuit set.
newsitem.headline: Refiling of Foster Wheeler lawsuit set.

text.p: Foster Wheeler Corp will refile its incinerator lawsuit against Illinois officials Friday in state court, an attorney representing the company said Thursday.
Chris Walsh, an attorney at Rothchild Barry & Meyer, said the lawsuit, which was dismissed Nov 1 in U.S. District Court in Chicago, will be refiled in Cook County Circuit Court.
He said the lawsuit will resemble the federal case and will also contain claims under state law.
Rick Redmond, an attorney at McBride Baker & Coles, who is representing state officials, said he would not comment on the refiled lawsuit until he sees it.

This latest move by Clinton, N.J.-based Foster Wheeler followed federal Judge James Zagel's ruling, which dismissed the lawsuit on the ground that the 11th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution precludes lawsuits against states dealing with public funds. Zagel said in the ruling that while Foster Wheeler's claims in the suit may have merit, the case should be litigated in state court and not federal court.
Walsh said Zagel's dismissal will also be appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals as early as next week.

Foster Wheeler filed the federal lawsuit against Gov. Jim Edgar and Illinois Commerce Commission members in the wake of Edgar's signing into law in March legislation repealing the state's Retail Rate Act. That act allowed waste-to-energy incinerators to sell electricity they produced to utilities at a higher rate subsidized by the state.
The lawsuit claimed that the repeal resulted in the unconstitutional impairment of contracts, and violated equal protection and due process constitutional provisions.

The lawsuit was filed by Foster Wheeler, its Illinois subsidiaries and the Chicago suburb of Robbins, where Foster Wheeler built an incinerator, financed with $320 million of unrated, tax-exempt bonds.

In October, Robbins completed a tender of nearly all of the bonds for new bonds with lower interest rates, some extended maturities, additional credit support from Foster Wheeler, new convenants and different redemption provisions.
Two other lawsuits filed by incinerator developers are also pending against Illinois officials in state courts.
